title: Of Miracles and Moats
gist: Packy McCormick argues the standard arguments against an AI bubble (real utility, fast revenue, lab profits) are just the first steps of the recurring miracle-technology capital cycle that ends in oversupply and price collapse, illustrated with railways, oil, autos, airlines and the fiber bandwidth bust. He is agnostic on Anthropic's ~$1.4T IPO and $900.9B compute commitments, but expects a huge consumer-surplus era in which only firms with durable moats and cost advantages (Rockefeller/Ford/Vanderbilt types) capture value.

themes.theme: Bubble-denial arguments are steps 1-3 of the capital cycle

insights.claim: The three common arguments that AI is not a bubble (genuinely useful tech, fast-growing real revenue, demonstrated lab profitability) are exactly the first three steps of the classic boom-bust capital cycle, so they do not refute a bubble.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Bull arguments about utility and revenue growth should not be read as evidence against overinvestment risk in AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: three of the main arguments you hear against AI being a bubble are steps one, two, and three

insights.claim: A miracle-technology cycle runs in ten steps: arrival, scarce early profits, seemingly bottomless demand, capital and competitor influx, simultaneous buildout at scarcity prices, supply arrival and price collapse, capital loses while consumers win, capital flees, a low-cost survivor consolidates, and demand catches up making the survivor larger than all failed firms combined.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Map any hot sector to its step in the cycle; the investable moment for consolidators comes after capital flees (step 8).
insights.quote: Supply arrives, the technology gets better, and prices collapse.

insights.claim: The first seven steps of the cycle are near-universal, but steps 8-10 (capital flight, consolidation by a low-cost survivor, demand catch-up) do not always happen; sometimes consumers simply consume the industry's corpses.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Do not assume a consolidation winner emerges in every glut; some industries (airlines) stay structurally unprofitable.
insights.quote: Sometimes consumers simply dine on the industry’s corpses.

insights.claim: The more incredible and scalable-by-capital a technology is, the more competitors it attracts, who in aggregate overbuild supply and crash prices; a miracle technology does not guarantee a miraculous business.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Capital-scalable technologies carry structurally higher glut risk for producers.
insights.quote: a miracle technology does not guarantee a miraculous business

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO and AI compute commitments

insights.claim: Anthropic is going public at roughly a $1.4 trillion valuation; the author says nobody can know whether it becomes a winner-take-all-markets giant or an overvalued commodity LLM forced to sell to Amazon or Apple.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The author is explicitly agnostic on the Anthropic IPO; position sizing should reflect a bimodal outcome.
insights.quote: Anyone who tells you they know which of those two outcomes will come to pass is full of shit
insights.locator: There is a world in which

insights.claim: Bear case for Anthropic: no new S-curve as intense as coding emerges, or competition from OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, Meta, Chinese open-source models and neolabs slows revenue growth enough that boom-time compute commitments force a sale.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Fixed long-dated compute commitments turn a modest growth miss into a solvency event.
insights.locator: There is a world in which

insights.claim: Bull case for Anthropic: it has the best models, they are improving themselves faster than ever, and the lead could be winner-take-all across every market Anthropic chooses to target, from productivity software to medicine.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If self-improvement compounds, AI lab value could extend across all software and service verticals.

insights.claim: Anthropic's S-1 reports $900.9 billion of compute commitments through 2045, about half expected before end of the decade, up from about $100 billion when Dario Amodei earlier called that level sensible.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A ~9x rise in fixed commitments raises the leverage of Anthropic's outcome to revenue growth.
insights.quote: Anthropic reported that it has now committed to $900.9 billion worth of compute through 2045

insights.claim: Dario Amodei said buying a trillion dollars a year of compute from end-2027 would bankrupt Anthropic if revenue came in at even $800 billion, illustrating that being off by a year on AI timelines is fatal.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Compute overcommitment is the key failure mode for AI labs, acknowledged by their own CEOs.
insights.quote: If you’re off by only a year, you destroy yourselves.

insights.claim: OpenAI told investors it targets about $600 billion in compute spend by 2030, down from a previously touted $1.4 trillion.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A downward revision in compute targets signals labs are already trimming overextended plans.

insights.claim: Anthropic generated an operating profit in Q2 and would have again in Q3 excluding roughly $2 billion of noncash donation-matching charges.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Lab profitability is real today, but per the framework, early profits are step 2 of the glut cycle.
insights.quote: Anthropic actually generated an operating profit in Q2

insights.claim: Anthropic's compute buildout resembles the British railways, American railways and even cannabis, where oversupply crashed prices; cannabis growers with powered industrial properties are now pivoting to AI data centers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Distressed power-rich real estate from other gluts may become cheap AI data-center supply, adding to compute oversupply.

insights.claim: In a race for a miracle technology, new entrants have nothing to lose and incumbents have everything to lose, so both rationally invest, producing aggregate overbuild even when participants foresee the glut.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Expect hyperscaler AI capex to keep rising regardless of bubble awareness; the brake will be capital markets, not management.
insights.quote: New entrants have nothing to lose and incumbents have everything to lose and both get you to the same place: you have to invest.

insights.claim: Google leadership explicitly frames AI capex asymmetrically: Sundar Pichai said the risk of underinvesting is dramatically greater than overinvesting, and Larry Page reportedly said he would rather go bankrupt than lose the race.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Google capex guidance is unlikely to be cut on ROI concerns alone.
insights.quote: the risk of underinvesting is dramatically greater than the risk of overinvesting

insights.claim: Mark Zuckerberg acknowledged AI may be a bubble and that Meta could misspend a couple hundred billion dollars, but judged the bigger risk is not being aggressive enough.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Meta, like Google, is pre-committed to overinvestment on strategic grounds.
insights.quote: The risk, at least for a company like Meta, is probably in not being aggressive enough rather than being somewhat too aggressive.

insights.claim: In 1846 Great Western Railway chairman Charles Russell urged Parliament to curb 'bubble schemes' while his own railway bought up rival lines 'in self-defence'; Parliament that year authorized 4,540 miles of new track after 1,263 proposed schemes.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Incumbents warning about bubbles while racing to build is a historical signature of the overbuild phase.
insights.quote: In 1846, Parliament passed acts authorizing 4,540 miles of new track.

insights.claim: Early British railways (Liverpool & Manchester, London & Birmingham) paid dividends of at least 10% in 1842 while supply was scarce, which drew in hundreds of competing schemes.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: High early returns on scarce infrastructure are the magnet for the eventual glut.

themes.theme: Fiber bandwidth bubble as AI analog

insights.claim: The dot-com bandwidth bubble should be separated from the internet stock mania: fiber builders were acting rationally on real exploding demand, but overbuilt capacity on optimistic early demand signals, which is the closer analogy for AI.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Dismissing dot-com comparisons because AI firms have real revenue misses the bandwidth precedent, where real demand still bankrupted builders.
insights.quote: It’s worth separating the internet stock mania from the bandwidth bubble

insights.claim: The famous 'internet traffic doubling every 100 days' statistic in a 1998 Commerce Department report actually traced back to WorldCom's buildout pace (supply), not demand; traffic in fact doubled roughly yearly.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Scrutinize AI demand metrics for supply-side numbers masquerading as demand.
insights.locator: It was hard to imagine where

insights.claim: U.S. long-haul fiber mileage doubled from 100k to 200k miles in 1996-2001 while electronics upgrades let each strand carry up to 40x more data, with about $500 billion spent on the buildout.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Supply grows multiplicatively (more capacity times efficiency gains); AI compute efficiency gains could compound overbuild similarly.
insights.quote: In total, telcos spent something like $500 billion on the buildout.

insights.claim: Bandwidth prices on major routes fell about 70% annually for three years; a 155 Mbps New York-Los Angeles circuit went from $1.8 million a year in 2000 to under $150,000 by early 2002.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Commodity capacity pricing can collapse >90% in two years once supply arrives; relevant for GPU/token pricing.

insights.claim: Qwest's market cap rose to $91 billion in 2000 and fell to $1.9 billion by August 2002, after its CEO had told investors Internet demand ensured there would be no bandwidth glut.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Management assurances that demand precludes a glut are a late-cycle signal.
insights.quote: The explosive demand driven by the Internet phenomenon ensures there won’t be a glut of bandwidth.

insights.claim: Global Crossing's network traffic grew 130% in the year it emerged from bankruptcy, yet revenue fell 6%, because bandwidth had lost its value; usage growth does not equal revenue growth in a glut.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Token or usage growth at AI providers can coexist with falling revenue if unit prices collapse.
insights.quote: Traffic on its network grew 130%! Problem was, bandwidth wasn’t worth what it once was. Its revenue fell 6%.
insights.locator: In the year that Global Crossing

insights.claim: Even the eventual winner Level 3, which built a cost advantage with 12 conduits and rolled up competitors with Buffett's backing, sold to CenturyLink in 2017 at a price 97% below its peak; picking the winner is not enough if entry price assumes away competition.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Valuation discipline matters even for the probable AI winner.
insights.quote: Even identifying the eventual winner might not matter if you pay entry prices that assume away the corrosive forces of competition.

themes.theme: Consolidators who win the glut: Rockefeller, Ford, Vanderbilt

insights.claim: Oil fell from $20 a barrel in 1860 to 50 cents by June 1861 and 10 cents by December as prospectors flooded in, despite near-bottomless demand; Pithole farmland sold for $2 million in 1865 was resold for $4.37 in 1878.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Correctly sizing the market does not protect investors from supply-side price collapse.
insights.locator: The fiber companies got a little

insights.claim: 1865-era oil investors got market sizing right but ignored competitive dynamics: ~600 petroleum companies sought $500 million of capital, and a single oil company later exceeded that entire value.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: TAM-based AI valuations miss the competitive dynamics question.
insights.quote: They got the market sizing right and ignored the competitive dynamics.
insights.locator: Investors were not wrong on the size

insights.claim: Rockefeller saw volatility as the constraint on oil profits and attacked it via scale, cost reduction, selling byproducts and vertical integration, reaching 90% of US refining by the 1880s; at its 1911 breakup Standard Oil's $1.1 billion market cap was ~6% of the US stock market.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The consolidator that anticipates the glut and becomes low-cost provider captures outsized value.
insights.quote: He anticipated the glut, and positioned himself to benefit from it.

insights.claim: About 2,000 US automakers existed in the car's first decades and nearly all failed; by the early 1940s Ford, GM and Chrysler sold 90% of cars, with Ford winning by being low-cost provider and using scale to lower prices further.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: In a glut, the scale-cost flywheel is the winning strategy.
insights.quote: in a glut, being the low cost provider of quality, using low prices to get to scale, and using scale to get even lower prices and more scale was how you win

insights.claim: Vanderbilt was technology-agnostic, moving from sailboats to steamships to rail while always seeking durable route advantages in speed and cost (Nicaragua route, Harlem Railroad into Manhattan), dying with wealth equal to ~1 in 20 dollars in US circulation.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Favor businesses that can swap in better underlying technology rather than being disrupted by it.

themes.theme: Consumer surplus and where moats survive

insights.claim: Nordhaus found producers captured only about 2.2% of the social surplus from innovation over 1948-2001, with consumers capturing roughly 97-98%.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Base rate: investors in transformational tech capture a tiny share of the value created.
insights.quote: only a miniscule fraction of the social returns from technological advances over the 1948-2001 period was captured by producers

insights.claim: Nordhaus attributed part of the New Economy bubble to investors overestimating the appropriability of innovations, i.e. what was built was valuable but investors could not capture it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The key AI investing question is appropriability, not usefulness.
insights.quote: investors overestimated the appropriability of innovations in that sector

insights.claim: When demand is obvious, only categories with restricted entry avoided the glut cycle: regulated industries (pharma, pre-1978 airlines), patents (Bell Telephone until 1894, Alcoa); when such cornered resources lapse, competition floods in.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Look for regulatory or IP-based entry barriers; absent them, assume commoditization.
insights.quote: These are Cornered Resources, and when they lapse, competition floods in and the same dynamics play out.
insights.locator: As I wrote in When to Dig a Moat

insights.claim: Other exceptions are cases where demand is non-obvious (Amazon hid AWS profits for nine years) or Process Power compounds over decades from risky bets (ASML); anything one can just throw money at is subject to the jungle, which favors consumers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Capital-insensitive advantages (process know-how, hidden economics) are the durable moats.
insights.quote: Opportunities where you can’t just throw money at the problem in order to compete, for one reason or another, are somewhat protected.

insights.claim: A key attraction of AI for investors—that you can just throw money at it—is precisely what makes it vulnerable to the overbuild cycle.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Capital-scalability is a bear signal for producer margins.
insights.quote: One of the things that investors love about AI is that you can just throw money at it.
insights.locator: One of the things that investors

insights.claim: AI makes other things easier to build, so the cycle should spread across industries; Anthropic used Claude models to weaken Nvidia's CUDA moat, reportedly letting a model run itself on AMD hardware in 3 days.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: AI accelerates imitation, eroding incumbent software moats such as CUDA and treating compute as fungible.
insights.locator: It also makes a lot of other

insights.claim: We are entering an unprecedented age of consumer surplus as booms run across AI, robotics, power, manufacturing and biotech; even new cancer cures get outcompeted by newer technologies within months.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Expect rapid price deflation and short product lifecycles across frontier tech sectors.
insights.quote: I think we are entering an age of consumer surplus the likes of which humanity has never seen
insights.locator: The net of it all is that

themes.theme: Investment stance: cost leaders that plug in new tech

insights.claim: McCormick favors Vanderbilt/Rockefeller/Ford-style companies that can plug in better technology or models to deliver a cheaper product, positioned to win whether the boom continues or a fire sale on miracle technologies arrives.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Prefer AI consumers/integrators with cost advantages over pure model or infrastructure producers.
insights.locator: I like companies that are like

insights.claim: As technology moves into the physical world, scale economies and cost advantages will matter more than the network effects that dominated the internet era.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Re-weight moat analysis toward cost curves and scale for physical-world AI businesses.
insights.quote: I suspect scale economies and cost advantages will be critical as technology once again reaches out into the physical world
insights.locator: I like companies that are like

insights.claim: Durable competitive advantage, plus entry price, determines whether investors profit from a technology's spread; the more miraculous the technology, the more crucial the moats.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Core screening rule for AI-era investments.
insights.quote: The more miraculous your technology, the more crucial your moats.

insights.claim: Buffett called airlines the worst business type—rapid growth, heavy capital, little profit—yet bought ~$7-8 billion of US airline stakes in 2016 and sold at a loss in April 2020, noting the aircraft don't disappear when demand falls.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Excess physical capacity outlives demand shocks; applies to data centers and GPUs.
